entities.name: The Polish-Lithuanian Corpus
entities.label: Text
entities.summary:
The Polish-Lithuanian Corpus encompasses the literary, legal, scientific, and historical output of the Polish Crown and the Grand Duchy of Lithuania — which formed the enormous Polish-Lithuanian Commonwealth (1569–1795), at its peak the largest state in Europe. Key works include: Jan Długosz's Annales seu Cronicae Incliti Regni Poloniae (Annals of Poland, 12 volumes, completed 1480) — the most comprehensive medieval chronicle of any Central European nation; the Nihil Novi act of 1505 ("nothing new [without the common consent]") — a constitutional milestone establishing that no laws could be passed without the agreement of the Sejm (parliament); the Statutes of Lithuania (three editions: 1529, 1566, 1588) — remarkable legal codes for the Grand Duchy, compiled in Chancery Slavonic/Polish; Nicolaus Copernicus's De Revolutionibus Orbium Coelestium (1543) — the heliocentric revolution, written at Frombork in Royal Prussia; and the literary legacy of Polish Golden Age humanism (Jan Kochanowski's Treny — elegiac laments, 1580, the finest lyric poetry in Renaissance Polish).

The Commonwealth's tradition of religious tolerance (Warsaw Confederation of 1573 — the first European act of religious freedom) and elective monarchy represents a unique political experiment.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Polish-Lithuanian Corpus played a pivotal role in shaping the Grand Duchy of Lithuania's legal and constitutional framework, with its Statutes of Lithuania serving as a model for subsequent European legal codes. Its impact can be seen in the development of modern nation-states.
